equityOrStake: Minority stake in Utah Brands & Entertainment LLC (UBE), a new for-profit company
structure: The University of Utah moved its athletics commercial business (media/multimedia rights, sponsorship, ticketing and premium seating, events, merchandise, NIL facilitation) into Utah Brands & Entertainment LLC. Otro Capital, the sports investment firm led by former Cleveland Browns/Dallas Cowboys executive Alec Scheiner and known for its 2023 Alpine F1 investment, bought a minority equity stake. The university keeps majority ownership and control of the athletic department: coaches, competition, compliance and academics.
strings: Otro gets board representation at UBE and a return from growth in commercial revenue: a cut of UBE profits and an eventual exit or recapitalization. Control of conference membership, scheduling and athlete matters stays with the university. Big 12 and state approval was needed.
returnExpectations: Not disclosed. Sports PE typically targets ~15-25% gross IRR (mid-teens net) over 5-7 years.
opposition: Some faculty, state political and fan concerns about commercializing a public university's athletics. No blocking opposition is known.
outcome: First Power 4 school-level private-equity deal. Seen as the template for other schools facing $20.5M+ House revenue-sharing costs.
note: Deal existence and the UBE name match the brief. Timing, size and governance details are from researcher recall and were not verified this session.

equityOrStake: Reported minority stake (~10-20%) in a Big 12 commercial-rights entity
structure: RedBird Capital Partners (Gerry Cardinale) and Weatherford Capital (the Weatherford brothers' Florida firm) formed Collegiate Athletic Solutions to invest in college sports. The proposal was up to ~$1B of capital into a new Big 12 commercial entity holding media, sponsorship and events rights. Schools could take upfront cash to fund House revenue sharing and facilities.
strings: Investor governance seats on the commercial entity. A share of future media-rights growth, which links returns to the next Big 12 media cycle (current deal through 2030-31). Some schools would likely have needed to extend their grants of rights.
returnExpectations: PE-style returns from media-rights escalation. Not disclosed.
opposition: Member presidents worried about giving up future revenue and ceding control. Commissioner Brett Yormark publicly supported exploring private capital.
outcome: No completed conference-level deal as of last verified reporting. The Big 12 kept talking with investors and leaned on corporate partnerships (naming and sponsorship deals) instead.
note: Amount and status are from researcher recall. The brief's 'what happened' could not be confirmed with a search this session.

equityOrStake: About 10% of a new for-profit 'Big Ten Enterprises' (some reports round to ~$2B)
structure: The Big Ten would move its media and commercial rights into Big Ten Enterprises. UC Investments, the University of California system's investment office (whose system includes Big Ten member UCLA), would invest about $2.4B for a minority stake. Member schools would receive upfront cash in unequal amounts, with larger brands reportedly getting more. Members would extend their grant of rights to about 2046.
strings: A 20-year GOR extension locks the league together. The investor gets a share of future media-revenue growth and governance and information rights. Tiered upfront payments would have ended the equal-share principle.
returnExpectations: A long-duration return tied to the Big Ten's media escalators, similar to an infrastructure or royalty investment.
opposition: Michigan (regents and athletics leadership) and USC objected to the long GOR term, the unequal payouts and selling future revenue. Commissioner Tony Petitti could not get the needed member support.
outcome: Shelved in late 2025 / early 2026. The Big Ten kept looking at other ways to raise capital. This matches the brief's 'failed ~$2B deal' framing.
note: The opposition from Michigan and USC and the ~$2.4B / Big Ten Enterprises framing are from researcher recall of fall-2025 reporting. Not re-verified this session.

equityOrStake: Discussed minority stakes in conference media/commercial rights
structure: CVC Capital Partners, investor in La Liga, Ligue 1 and Six Nations rugby commercial rights, pitched college conferences on buying a minority stake in a commercial-rights company for upfront cash. Its European model buys ~10% of league media revenue for decades. Earlier, in 2021-22, the Pac-12 under George Kliavkoff had explored private-equity options for its media rights and network.
strings: Long or permanent revenue participation (the La Liga deal is 50 years). Investor seats on commercial boards.
returnExpectations: Like CVC's sports-league deals: a long-dated share of revenue growth.
opposition: The Pac-12 collapsed before any deal (Aug 2023). The Big 12 did not proceed.
note: Dates and parties follow the brief and researcher recall. Not verified.

equityOrStake: Proposed central commercial entity / super-league structure
structure: Elevate, the sports and entertainment agency also tied to Velocity Capital, and Collegiate Sports Management Group (CSMG) pitched consolidating top-tier college football's commercial rights into a new private company. CSMG's plan was branded 'College Sports Tomorrow' and proposed a 70+ team top division with a central media deal and revenue sharing. Private capital would fund upfront payments to schools.
strings: Investors get a share of centralized media revenue. Schools give up conference-level control, with a new governance structure outside the NCAA.
returnExpectations: Based on lifting college football media value toward NFL-like centralization.
opposition: Conference commissioners (especially the SEC and Big Ten) prefer keeping their own media deals and the CFP structure.
outcome: No adoption. These pitches remain a background force (super-league threat).
note: Names and branding are from researcher recall. Not verified this session.

equityOrStake: Explored private capital to finance an ACC exit (exit fee + GOR buyout reported at $500M+)
structure: FSU trustees publicly discussed leaving the ACC (Aug 2023), and the school sounded out private-equity and financial firms about funding the exit and litigation costs in exchange for a future revenue participation. Clemson looked at similar options as it sued the ACC (Mar 2024).
strings: A share of future media revenue at a new conference.
opposition: The ACC sued both schools to enforce the GOR.
outcome: Overtaken by the March 2025 settlement with the ACC, which reduced exit costs and created brand-based revenue distribution. No PE deal closed.
note: PE-exploration details are from researcher recall.

structure: Arctos Partners, the largest minority-stake investor in pro franchises (NBA, MLB, NHL, MLS, European football), was among the sports-specialist funds reported to be studying college athletics and conference commercial rights after House.
returnExpectations: Arctos-style minority stakes target low-to-mid-teens returns from franchise value appreciation.
note: Included because the brief lists it. Specific talks were not verified.

structure: Sixth Street, the credit-focused firm behind the Real Madrid stadium financing, FC Barcelona media-rights deals and its San Antonio Spurs stake, was reported among firms offering structured capital (debt/royalty-style financing against future media revenue) to conferences and schools.
strings: A royalty-style claim on future media payments rather than equity control.
note: Included because the brief lists it. Specific talks were not verified.

structure: Kentucky moved its athletic department into a university-controlled LLC to speed up decisions on revenue sharing, NIL and commercial deals, and to allow outside investment later.
outcome: The model has been copied or studied by other schools. It is a precondition for Utah-style PE deals.

equityOrStake: None. Booster philanthropy and collective (Matador Club) funding, not private equity.
structure: Energy billionaire Cody Campbell, chair of the Texas Tech System Board of Regents, funds Texas Tech NIL and roster spending at Power 4-leading levels and lobbies on federal college-sports legislation. It is the main counterexample to institutional PE: a single booster acting as the school's capital source.
strings: Influence over hiring and strategy rather than contractual governance rights.
opposition: Concerns about booster control and CSC/NIL Go scrutiny of payments from associated entities.
note: The brief asked whether Texas Tech had a PE deal. None was found; recorded as booster capital. No verified 2025-26 PE deals at LSU or Kansas were found.
